lesson_title: The Wave in the Stands: Transverse Waves and Their Quantities
hook_text: The stadium wave goes right around the ground — and nobody walks anywhere. That's physics.
clip_script: Packed stadium, Saturday afternoon. One section stands, throws their arms up, sits down. The next section copies. And a wave runs all the way around the ground. Now watch what actually moved. Nobody walked. Every person went straight UP and straight DOWN and sat back in the same seat — but the wave went SIDEWAYS. Movement one way, wave the other way, at right angles. That is a transverse wave, and a rope does exactly the same thing. What travelled around that stadium was not people. It was energy, handed from seat to seat. Now measure it. How high they throw their arms — that's amplitude, from the rest line to the top, never top to bottom. How far apart the ripples sit — that's wavelength. How many ripples pass you each second — that's frequency. How long one takes — that's the period, and it is just the frequency flipped over. Four a second means a quarter of a second each. And the whole equation? In one second you send off f humps, each one lambda long. So the wave advances f times lambda every second. That is the speed. v equals f lambda. You just derived it in a stadium.
visual_style: A packed South African stadium seen from high up, the wave sweeping round in gold; the crowd dissolves into a rope, then into a ripple tank, with amplitude and wavelength drawn as clean measuring arrows.
mood: Loud crowd energy resolving into calm, confident clarity.
pacing: Big roaring opener, a still beat on 'nobody walked', then brisk measured build to the equation.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never lose a mark on amplitude or period again.
